question: Does Statement 8 give hidden-watermark tooling and watermark-risk assessment the same required status as visual watermarks and metadata?
draft:
No. Under Statement 8, visual watermarks/metadata and AI-interaction disclosures are **Required**, while hidden-watermark tooling and watermark-risk assessment are **Recommended**.

**Required (Agencies must):**
- Criterion 22: Apply visual watermarks and metadata to generated media content to provide transparency and provenance, including authorship — applicable only where AI-generated content may directly impact a user (e.g., a generated team logo would not need watermarking) [1].
- Criterion 23: Apply watermarks and metadata that are WCAG compatible where relevant [1].
- Criterion 24: Apply visual and accessible content to indicate when a user is interacting with an AI system (e.g., text in a GenAI interface) [2].

**Recommended (Agencies should):**
- Criterion 25: For hidden watermarks, use watermarking tools based on the use case and content risk — including provenance/authorship information, encrypting watermarks for high-risk content, using an existing tool or technique when practicable, embedding watermarks at the AI training stage, verifying the watermark does not impact content generation quality or efficiency, and including data sources and product/versioning details [2].
- Criterion 26: Assess watermarking risks and limitations — including user understanding of third-party replication risk and avoiding over-reliance, preventing third-party use of watermarking algorithms, considering situations where watermarking is not beneficial, considering malicious removal or replication, and managing copyright/trademark risks from externally sourced data [3].

This Required/Recommended split is corroborated by the lifecycle summary listing Statement 8's criteria 22–24 as Required and criteria 25–26 as Recommended [4].

**Evidence gaps:** The available excerpts do not establish any additional conditions, exceptions, or deadlines attaching specifically to criteria 25–26 beyond those quoted.

child_citations.title: Australian Government AI Technical Standard
child_citations.quote:
Statement 10: Adopt a human-centred approach Agencies must: Criterion 32: Identify human values requirements. Human values represent what people deem important in life such as autonomy, simplicity, tradition, achievement, and social recognition. Refer to human value requirements for AI systems paper. This includes: o using traditional requirement elicitation techniques such as surveys, interviews, group discussions and workshops to capture relevant human values for the AI use case o translating human values into technical requirements, which may vary depending on the risk level and AI use case o reviewing feedback to identify ignored human-values in the AI system o understanding the hierarchy of human values and emphasising those with higher relevance o considering social, economic, political, ethical, and legal values when designing AI systems o considering human values that are domain specific and based on the context of the AI system. Criterion 33: Establish a mechanism to inform users of AI interactions and output, as part of transparency.

Depending on use case this may include: o incorporating visual cues on the AI product when applicable o informing users when text, audio or visual messages addressed to them are generated by AI o including visual watermarks to identify content generated by AI o providing transparency on whether a user is interacting with a person, or system o including a disclaimer on the limitations of the system o displaying the relevance and currency of the information being provided o persona level transparency adhering to need-to-know principles

child_citations.title: Australian Government AI Technical Standard
child_citations.quote: Whole of AI lifecycle Whole of AI lifecycle includes statements that apply across multiple AI product lifecycle stages, for ease of use and to minimise content duplication. Across the lifecycle stages, agencies should consider: • operational model – to ensure compliance, efficiency, and ethical standards • reference architecture – to provide structured frameworks that guide the design, development, and management of AI systems • people capabilities – having the specialised skills required for successful implementation • auditability – enabling external scrutiny, supporting transparency, and accountability • explainability – identifying what needs to be explained and when, making complex AI processes transparent and trustworthy • system bias – maintaining the role of positive bias in delivering meaningful outcomes, while mitigating the source and impacts of problematic bias • version control – tracking and managing changes to information to inform stakeholder decision-making • watermarking – to embed visual or hidden markers into generated content so that its creation details can be identified. NOTE: Agencies must consider intellectual property rights and ownership derived from procured services or datasets used (including general AI outputs) to comply with copyright law | ag.gov.au. NOTE: Management of bias in an AI system is critical to ensuring compliance with Australia’s anti-discrimination law | ag.gov.au.

child_citations.quote:

Criterion 19: Use metadata in version control to distinguish between production and non-production data, models, and code. This includes: o a simple and transparent way for all users of the system to understand the version of each component at the time a decision was made o the use of tags in the version number to provide a visual representation of non- production versions without needing direct access to data or source control toolsets o the use of metadata can also distinguish between different control states where outputs can vary, and core system functionality of the system has not changed. Criterion 20: Use a version control toolset to improve useability for users. Version toolsets improve the usability for service delivery and business users, addressing activities such as appeals, Ministerial correspondence, executive briefs, court cases, audit, assurance, privacy, and legislative reviews. This includes: o using purpose built in-house or commercial version management products o storing sufficient information to allow rollback to a previous system state o considering archival requirements of training data used in a test environment.

Criterion 7: Build and maintain AI capabilities by undertaking regular training and education of end users, staff, and stakeholders. This may involve: o agencies should provide regular training programs keep staff updated on the latest tools, methodologies, ethical guidelines and regulatory requirements o consider how to tailor training to the knowledge requirements of each role and provide staff involved in procurement, design, development, testing, and deployment of AI systems with specialised training. For example, individuals responsible for managing and operating AI decision-making systems should undergo specific AI ethics training o consider tailoring training for people with disability o consider interactive workshops, simulations, case study walk-throughs and computing sandpit environments to provide more immersive and real-world-like experiences especially for more complex aspects of AI. Agencies should: Criterion 8: Mitigate staff over-reliance, under-reliance, and aversion of AI. This may involve: o perform periodic technology-specific training, performance assessments, peer reviews, or random audits o implement a regular feedback loop for incorrect AI outcomes.
